Genoa at the centre is the chart's name for the decades, roughly 1557 to 1627, when bankers of the Republic of Genoa, by lending to the king of Spain, steered Europe's money and the flow of American silver. Fernand Braudel calls it the age of the Genoese, when the centre of the European economy was not a busy port but a handful of financiers.

Genoa was an old maritime republic that had lost its eastern trade to Venice and the Ottomans. Its merchants turned to finance. When the Spanish crown went bankrupt in 1557, ruining its German lenders, Genoese bankers took their place.

How it worked:

  • Spain's armies in the Netherlands and Italy needed steady pay in gold. The crown's income came in silver, in irregular fleets from America.
  • Genoese bankers lent the king money where and when he needed it, against future silver from Potosí and Mexico arriving at Seville.
  • They settled their accounts at the fairs of Piacenza, where bills of exchange from across Europe were cleared.

Genoa itself stayed small and quiet; the money moved on paper. The end date marks the Spanish bankruptcy of 1627, after which the crown turned to Portuguese lenders. By then the real growth was in the north, and the centre passed to Amsterdam.
